claims.text: The initial alloy is a rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy.
The initial microstructure is a homogeneous metastable solid solution in which Mg and the other elements are uniformly dispersed.
Intermetallic precipitates are minimal or absent in the initial state.
Slow diffusional decomposition during service nucleates and grows Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
Isothermal aging promotes the diffusional kinetics responsible for phase separation.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates initially form from the metastable solid solution.
A fine dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates supports a continuous protective oxide scale.
Maintaining finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates preserves corrosion resistance.
Maintaining finely dispersed intermetallic precipitates preserves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Coarsening beyond a critical precipitate size or volume fraction produces intermetallic networks that disrupt the protective oxide or passivating layer.
Disruption of the protective layer by coarsened intermetallics accelerates corrosion.
Disruption of the protective layer by coarsened intermetallics accelerates oxidation.
The proposed service transition between benign precipitation and deleterious coarsening is expected within 550–650 °C during prolonged exposure, such as exposure exceeding 100 hours.
The initial metastable state has established baseline corrosion resistance.
The initial metastable state has established baseline high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Aging at approximately 600 °C over durations spanning nucleation and coarsening regimes is proposed as the experimental intervention.
A lower-temperature control is proposed to inhibit diffusion relative to the aged samples.
Failure of corrosion and oxidation behavior to correlate with intermetallic evolution would falsify the hypothesis.
